good_sentence: Never have I seen such a mess.
bad_sentence: Never I have seen such a mess.
notes: A fronted 'never' forces subject-aux inversion; the uninverted 'I have' order is ungrammatical.

good_sentence: Rarely does he speak in meetings.
bad_sentence: Rarely he speaks in meetings.
notes: Fronted 'rarely' requires do-support and inversion; the plain 'he speaks' order fails to invert.

good_sentence: Seldom had they faced such odds.
bad_sentence: Seldom they had faced such odds.
notes: After fronted 'seldom' the auxiliary must precede the subject; 'they had' is the uninverted, bad order.

good_sentence: Hardly had she arrived when it started.
bad_sentence: Hardly she had arrived when it started.
notes: Fronted 'hardly' triggers obligatory inversion; the subject 'she' cannot precede the auxiliary 'had'.

good_sentence: Scarcely could we hear the announcement.
bad_sentence: Scarcely we could hear the announcement.
notes: The fronted restrictive 'scarcely' forces 'could' before the subject; the uninverted order is ungrammatical.

good_sentence: Barely did the engine start.
bad_sentence: Barely the engine started.
notes: Fronted 'barely' requires do-support inversion; the plain past 'the engine started' fails to invert.

good_sentence: Not only did she win, she set a record.
bad_sentence: Not only she won, she set a record.
notes: Fronted 'not only' triggers subject-aux inversion; 'she won' without do-support is ungrammatical.

good_sentence: No sooner had we left than it rained.
bad_sentence: No sooner we had left than it rained.
notes: The fronted 'no sooner' requires the auxiliary before the subject; 'we had' is the uninverted, bad order.

good_sentence: Nowhere have I felt so welcome.

good_sentence: Little did they know what awaited them.
